newsitem.title: USA: Conn. gets preliminary pact with unions - paper.
newsitem.headline: Conn. gets preliminary pact with unions - paper.

text.p: Connecticut has reached a pension and health-care settlement with its unions that could save more than $140 million over the next two years, Hartford Courant reported Tuesday.
But the agreement must be approved by the legislature and 11 unions, who represent about 43,000 employees. Another 9,000 nonunion employees would also be affected.
Connecticut, which wanted a tougher deal, has incorporated the projected savings into the budget proposal that Gov. John Rowland is due to present to the legislature Feb 13.

Under the pact, state employees and retirees would be able to choose a health insurance plan that pays for 100 percent of their coverage, but employees would be able to select from five plans that range from managed-care to the most expensive idemnity plan, the paper said.

The state first had sought to have union members and retirees pay 30 percent of their health care premiums. It now pays for 100 percent of the coverage for individuals but requires 30 percent co-payments for family members.
In the first year, the savings are projected to amount to about $33 million, followed by $111 million in the second year and $116 million in the third year, the paper said.
While the state would change its mechanism for funding payments in to the pension fund, the overall liability for the state would stay the same, it added.
